posts: We consulted staff, students and parents for a year before this decision. The data on disruption and wellbeing convinced us. We're ready to listen to real problems at the info evening—this is about schools being calm learning spaces, not control.

Medical exemption requests close 1 August. If your child monitors glucose, needs an inhaler alert, or has another health reason—email me early with your GP or nurse's letter. The process works smoothly when we have time to set it up.

Twelve years teaching and I can't count how many times a phone buzz stops an entire lesson. I'm hopeful this works, but it will only stick if all staff enforce it consistently. Our workload during transition matters too.

I've got no problem with less phone time in lessons. But if my daughter's after-school plans change and I can't reach her directly after 3pm, we've got a problem. How does the emergency contact thing actually work?

My grandson has type 1 diabetes and his phone is medical equipment. Duarte processed our exemption in days and he'll be safe. If you've got a medical concern, contact the pastoral lead early—it absolutely works.

Banning phones all day is easy policy-making. Teaching teenagers to manage their own device use—that's harder and actually useful for adult life. Sixth-formers still aren't trusted. Seems like avoidance to me.

posts: We consulted staff, students and parents for a year before this decision. The data on disruption and wellbeing convinced us. We're ready to listen to real problems at the info evening—this is about schools being calm learning spaces, not control.

Medical exemption requests close 1 August. If your child monitors glucose, needs an inhaler alert, or has another health reason—email me early with your GP or nurse's letter. The process works smoothly when we have time to set it up.

Twelve years teaching and I can't count how many times a phone buzz stops an entire lesson. I'm hopeful this works, but it will only stick if all staff enforce it consistently. Our workload during transition matters too.

I've got no problem with less phone time in lessons. But if my daughter's after-school plans change and I can't reach her directly after 3pm, we've got a problem. How does the emergency contact thing actually work?

My grandson has type 1 diabetes and his phone is medical equipment. Duarte processed our exemption in days and he'll be safe. If you've got a medical concern, contact the pastoral lead early—it absolutely works.

Banning phones all day is easy policy-making. Teaching teenagers to manage their own device use—that's harder and actually useful for adult life. Sixth-formers still aren't trusted. Seems like avoidance to me.
Exactly my worry too. My son's on the bus 40 mins each way—if plans change or he's stuck, I need to reach him. Has anyone actually asked the school HOW this works in practice?
I want to support this, but the emergency contact question keeps nagging at me. What's the actual process if my kid needs me in the afternoon? Not just 'contact us'—what are the protocols?

My daughter has type 1 diabetes and uses a phone monitor. Duarte's process was straightforward—email early with medical docs and it's sorted. The emergency contact thing deserves a clear answer though, ask at the info evening.
I see your point about Sixth Form, but in my work with teenagers, the real benefit is reducing social pressure and online harassment during the day. That's a skill worth building early.

A year of consultation but you're telling me to come to an info evening to raise 'real problems'? That's not listening, that's rubber-stamping. My shifts change daily. This policy doesn't work for families like mine.
The school has an emergency contact system—I'd just ask Duarte directly about the after-school process. They've been brilliant with my grandson's exemption, so I trust them on this too.

We appreciate Leon's point about self-regulation. The council pressed for sixth-form flexibility and emergency protocols precisely because of concerns like this. We'll be monitoring implementation and welcome detailed feedback at the info evening.

A year of consultation is great, but where's the evidence that confiscation teaches anything? You're solving a symptom (disruption) not building the skill (self-regulation) they'll need at uni and beyond.
We hear you—shift work makes this harder. The info evening is genuinely for questions like yours, not a rubber stamp. Come with specifics on what timing would work and we'll take it to leadership.
Exactly—shift work is inflexible. My son's bus commute isn't a choice either. We shouldn't have to guess at emergency protocols. School needs to publish the actual process before the info evening.
I get your worry—Duarte's team has been so responsive with my grandson's needs that I'm confident they'll sort the emergency thing too. Worth asking them directly rather than waiting.
I appreciate the honesty on monitoring, but 'will monitor implementation' doesn't address my core point: are you building self-regulation or just deferring the problem to university?

Claire, fair question. Emergency protocols: if your child needs to reach you, they speak to reception or pastoral. Staff have a phone line for genuine medical/safety needs. We'll detail this at the info evening—I want it clear for every parent.
Leon, I get the self-regulation point. But in practice? Phones interrupt every lesson. If this policy gives us back even 20 mins of focused teaching time, that *is* building a skill—concentration.
Claire, the emergency protocols question is fair. I'd push Amara on specifics at the info evening—we need staff clear on this too, not just parents.
Today's bus incident reinforced why our emergency protocols matter. We'll publish detailed procedures before the info evening. Parents deserve clarity, not just assurance.
Today's bus breakdown on the motorway—students safely accounted for, staff responded well. But this shows why clear emergency protocols matter. We're publishing detailed procedures by end of week.
The bus breakdown today highlighted exactly what we've been asking about. We're pushing leadership to publish emergency protocols this week—parents need answers before September.
The bus breakdown today shows the gap between our protocols and reality. Staff handled it well, but we need Amara to publish the actual emergency contact process NOW, not at the info evening.
Today's bus incident proves the emergency protocols debate wasn't theoretical. Good to see staff handled it, but this reinforces why we need published procedures, not promises.

A school bus breaks down and students can't call home for an hour because their phones are locked away. This is the scenario I've been asking about. The school promised 'protocols'—where were they today?

Headteacher, today's bus breakdown showed the emergency protocols aren't working yet. Kids couldn't reach parents. Before the info evening, the school needs to show these protocols actually function under pressure, not just in theory.
Just heard about the bus breakdown. Students stuck for over an hour with no way to call home. This is exactly what parents have been saying would happen. Hope everyone's okay.

Parents are right. The bus incident exposed a gap between our protocols and reality. We're publishing detailed emergency procedures by Friday—not promises, written step-by-step processes. Parents deserve clarity.
Jamal, exactly right. We're escalating this to leadership today—parents need to see written protocols before the info evening, not promises. The bus incident proved the gap.

Supporting you on this, Amara. Parents need the emergency protocols written clearly—not just for reassurance, but so our staff can implement them consistently. I'm ready to help draft the after-school contact pathway.
Ms Okafor, thank you—you're saying what I've been asking all along. The protocols need to be written, tested, and published NOW. Parents can't make decisions on promises.
Amara, 'by end of week' isn't soon enough. Parents need to see the actual written procedures before the info evening—not discuss them, see them. The bus proved my concerns were real.
Appreciate the commitment, Amara, but parents need those protocols in writing before September, not just promised at the info evening. Today showed the gap between theory and practice.
I trust Duarte and the team—they handled my grandson's exemption brilliantly. But Claire and others need to see the actual written protocols, not just get told they exist. Fair to push for that.

Claire, I understand the frustration. Today showed the gap between theory and practice. But Lewis has committed to publishing procedures by Friday—let's hold them to it and get clear answers at the info evening.
Emergency procedures draft is with Duarte now—circulation to staff and parents council by Thursday evening, publication Friday morning. This has to be done right, not fast.
Amara, the council will review Thursday evening and help circulate to parents before Friday publication. We'll make sure this reaches everyone before the info evening.
Good. 'Written step-by-step' is what matters. But also: once these are published, the school needs to actually train staff and test them under pressure before September, not just hand out a document.
Leon, you're absolutely right. Publishing the procedures is essential but not sufficient. We're planning staff training in late August—I'll send detail on that separately to all staff.
Parents: the detailed emergency procedures will reach you Friday morning. The council will share widely before the info evening. Read them carefully—your feedback still matters.
Leon's right—publishing is only step one. Staff need proper training on these protocols, not just the document. I'll push for a staff briefing before Sept 1st.
Good timeline. But Amara, once staff have the procedures, will you commit to a staff drill—actually test these protocols under simulated pressure before day one? Otherwise it's just paper.

Emergency procedures published this morning. Full protocol for student contact during incidents now available on our website and shared with parents council. Thank you for the feedback that made this urgent.
